solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Traitor bitter perhaps about carrying board (8)

indicatorNotes.about: BEER goes about, round, the next piece

blocks.note: bitter is a kind of beer, hence 'perhaps'
a tray is a flat board for carrying food

annotation.surface: A turncoat is spotted at the pub, pint of bitter in hand, carrying something to the table.
annotation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British pale ale, so it stands for BEER by example. BE + TRAY + ER.
annotation.definitionFit: A betrayer is one who betrays, which is exactly what a traitor does.

blocks.note: to stretch a rope taut, or overstretch a muscle
a passage of music, as in the snatches of a waltz drifting in

annotation.walkthrough: Two words, two unrelated senses of one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are standard senses: strain as over-stretching, and strain as a passage of music.

indicatorNotes.turning: the letters turn about into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A mob boss turns his guns on a royal residence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turning on' reads as a phrasal verb meaning attacking, but 'on' is fodder and 'turning' alone is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Al Capone was the Chicago gangster of the Prohibition era.

indicatorNotes.situated in: the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the last two letters of the first word plus the first two of the second

annotation.surface: A geography note: a region located in the Far East.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a plain statement of fact, which is exactly why the letters sitting across 'Far East' are easy to read past.
annotation.definitionFit: An area and a region are both a stretch of land or territory.

entries.clue: Drink freely on lake ride in US (8)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, A on B puts A above B

blocks.note: to carouse is to drink freely and noisily
L is the standard abbreviation for lake

annotation.surface: Someone drinks too much at a lakeside and then gets on a fairground ride in America.
annotation.walkthrough: The British call this ride a merry-go-round or roundabout; 'carousel' is the American word, hence 'in US'.
annotation.definitionFit: A carousel is the fairground ride of painted horses that go round and round.

entries.clue: Called up somebody to interrupt Doctor of Philosophy (6)

indicatorNotes.to interrupt: ONE breaks into the middle of PHD

blocks.note: PhD is the degree Doctor of Philosophy
one = somebody, as in 'one does one's best'

annotation.surface: Someone rings and breaks in on a learned doctor at work.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer really does describe interrupting by phone, so the surface and the definition tell the same story.
annotation.definitionFit: To call someone up is to phone them.

entries.clue: Require newspaper man to go after leaders of Nigeria and Egypt (4)

indicatorNotes.leaders of: take the first letter of each word
indicatorNotes.to go after: ED is placed after those two letters

blocks.note: first letters of Nigeria and Egypt
ED = editor, the man in charge of a newspaper

annotation.surface: A news organisation wants a reporter to follow the heads of two African states.
annotation.walkthrough: ED for editor is a crossword staple.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs say something is necessary to you, as in 'we require more time'.

blocks.note: to beat is to outdo or surpass
a casino regular is someone who places wagers

annotation.surface: A regular at a casino gets beaten up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beat' reads as the past tense of an assault on the gambler, but it is the verb in the present: to better is to beat.
annotation.definitionFit: Better as a verb means outdo or beat; as a noun it is anyone who places bets.

entries.clue: Where one finds studs and peer with multiple awards (8)

blocks.note: an earl is a peer of the realm
OBE is the British honour Officer of the Order of the British Empire; several are OBES

annotation.surface: A stud farm, or a society page about a much-decorated aristocrat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Studs' suggests breeding horses and 'peer' a lord, both pulling towards country estates, but the studs are earrings.
annotation.definitionFit: Stud earrings are worn through the earlobes.

blocks.note: or is gold in heraldry
CA is the postal abbreviation for California

annotation.surface: A danger lurking off the Golden State's coast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Golden California' suggests the Golden State nickname, but the two words are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: The orca, or killer whale, is a top predator of the sea.

indicatorNotes.of some: the answer is some of the next word

blocks.note: the three letters after the opening M

annotation.surface: A question about what museums are for.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks what purpose some museums serve; the answer is lying in the word itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both nouns name what an object is for, its purpose.

indicatorNotes.ruined: the letters of the fodder are wrecked into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A poisoning spoils a spell of fine weather.
annotation.walkthrough: The anagram indicator sits between the definition and the fodder, so it reads as a verb in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: these carbon-nitrogen compounds are among the deadliest toxins known, and the plural matches.

blocks.note: D is the standard abbreviation for Democrat
ejected = kicked out

annotation.surface: A Democrat politician is unhappy at being thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a neat story: getting kicked out would indeed make one dejected.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both adjectives describe someone low in spirits, downcast.

entries.clue: Ahead of time, king or queen possibly returned money owed (4)

indicatorNotes.returned: BED is turned back to DEB
indicatorNotes.Ahead of: DEB is placed in front of T

blocks.note: king-size and queen-size are sizes of bed
T is the standard abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: A monarch comes back early to settle what is owed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'King or queen' points at royalty, but they are bed sizes, hence 'possibly'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain descriptive phrase: whatever sum you still have to pay back to a lender is exactly this.

indicatorNotes.Hacked: the fodder is chopped up and rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A computer server in Bali has been hacked.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hacked' and 'server' set up a computing story; the server is a tennis player, who serves from behind the baseline. The question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: In tennis the server stands behind the baseline, the line at the back of the court.

indicatorNotes.according to hearsay: the answer is what one hears, not what is written

blocks.note: bread is slang for money, as is moolah

annotation.surface: Someone has raised cash, or so the gossip goes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Raised' looks like fund-raising next to 'moolah', but it means brought up.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both past participles mean brought up, as in the idiom 'born and raised'.

entries.clue: Hang loosely some letters from Brendan Gleeson (6)

indicatorNotes.some letters from: the answer is a run of letters taken from the name

blocks.note: six letters straddling the gap: the end of the first name and the start of the surname

annotation.surface: Brendan Gleeson, the Irish actor, is hanging about in some fan mail.
annotation.walkthrough: The indicator almost announces itself here; the trick is spanning the break between first name and surname.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe something suspended and swinging free, like keys on a chain.

entries.clue: Most entertaining stories found in jar (8)

blocks.note: a jar is a jolt, a sudden shake
to tell stories is to tell lies

annotation.surface: The funniest tales turn up in a jar, like notes in a keepsake pot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jar' looks like a container, but it is the verb or noun meaning jolt; the container here is the word JOLT.
annotation.definitionFit: Jolliest means merriest, the most fun to be around.

blocks.note: in = fashionable, popular
a vent is an outlet for air or steam

annotation.surface: Advice to build a shop that people will like.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Popular outlet' suggests a busy shop; the two words are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to bring something new into being.

blocks.note: a cassette is a tape; its first letter T is dropped

annotation.surface: A mimic's recorded act goes wrong when the tape won't play.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Failing to start' sounds like a jammed tape machine, which suits the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: To ape is to mimic, so an ape is an imitator, as in 'copycat'.

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, lifting the T moves it to the top

blocks.note: a riot is a free-for-all, four letters ending in T
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature; it is the letter that rises to the top

annotation.surface: Tempers run hot in a brawl among a gang.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temperature raised' sounds like heat rising in a fight; in a down entry 'raised' moves the T up to the start.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: any band or set of three people is one particular kind of group.

blocks.note: on = covering, as a lid is on a pot
L = large, the clothing size
Y is the abbreviation for yard

annotation.surface: A modest claim about paving a big garden.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covering' looks like a container indicator, but it simply supplies ON.
annotation.definitionFit: Only and just are interchangeable, as in 'only/just a minute'.

blocks.note: ville is French for town; its middle letter L is the heart that goes

annotation.surface: A corrupt town in France has lost its soul.
annotation.walkthrough: VILLE has five letters, so its heart is the single central L.
annotation.definitionFit: Vile and depraved both mean morally wicked.

entries.clue: Cheer up English resort town, I say (8)

indicatorNotes.I say: the answer is how the town is said, not spelt

blocks.note: Brighton is a seaside resort on England's south coast

annotation.surface: An exclamation urging someone to perk up, since there's always a trip to the seaside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I say' reads as a British exclamation of surprise, but it signals that the town is to be spoken.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to become or make more cheerful, as a face does at good news.

entries.clue: Empty lockers holding nine torn sheets? (6)

indicatorNotes.Empty: take away the inside of the word, leaving L and S
indicatorNotes.holding: L...S hold the anagram between them
indicatorNotes.torn: NINE is torn into a new order

blocks.note: LOCKERS with the middle removed
anagram of NINE

annotation.surface: Bare cupboards found to contain nine ripped bedsheets.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is there because sheets are only one example of linens, which also include tablecloths and towels.
annotation.definitionFit: Linens are household textiles such as bed sheets.

entries.clue: Remove wet Conservative accommodating metalworking union (5-3)

blocks.note: a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative party
a weld is a joint made by fusing metal

annotation.surface: A feeble Conservative politician is ousted after siding with a metalworkers' trade union.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wet' is British slang for a weak moderate Tory and 'union' suggests a trade union; here wet is wetness and the union is a weld.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful phrase: rubbing hair or dishes with a cloth takes the wet away, so the definition describes the action.
